I give up. I did not change `/work/putnam_2024_b6.lean`, and it still contains the `sorry`.

The statement is true, with the answer c = -1/2. The heuristic: with x = e^{-t}, the terms n^a e^{2n - t n²} peak at n ≈ 1/t, where the exponent is 1/t. A Gaussian approximation gives F_a(x) ≈ C · t^{-a-1/2} · e^{1/t}. Since 1/t and 1/(1-x) differ by a bounded amount, F_a(x) · e^{-1/(1-x)} behaves like a constant times t^{-a-1/2}. That tends to 0 when a < -1/2 and to ∞ when a > -1/2.

A Lean proof needs more than this heuristic:

- **Two-sided bounds, uniform in x near 1.** It needs an upper bound on the whole series, using decay away from the peak, and a lower bound from a window of about t^{-1/2} terms near n ≈ 1/t. Both must carry the correct polynomial factor t^{-a-1/2}.
- **Conversion between t = -log x and 1 - x.** The relation 1/(-log x) = 1/(1-x) - 1/2 + o(1) has to be proved and used.
- **Both directions of the iff.** For the reverse implication, I would need the asymptotics for every a ≠ -1/2 to rule out any other c. Showing the conditions force c = -1/2 means comparing limits at two different exponents, so the forward asymptotics alone are not enough.

Mathlib has the pieces needed (HasSum, comparison of series with integrals, real exponentials), but assembling these bounds in this environment, with only the compiler to check against, is a multi-hundred-line effort that I was not able to finish here.
